lines: Picture a worker holding onto some data it already cached, keeping it close for later.
Now a brand new piece of work shows up, and it genuinely needs room of its own to get anything done.
Both of them are reaching into the exact same pot.
Here's the shape of that pot, before anything happens to it.
It isn't two separate containers sitting side by side. It's one shared space, carved out of the whole, with a single line drawn somewhere inside it to mark where one use gives way to the other.
That line is the entire story of how the two sides divide what they've got.
Let that cached data grow well past whatever minimum share it's supposed to be owed.
Then let a real piece of work show up needing its own room.
steps.answer: It doesn't hold its ground at all. Nothing about already being cached protects space that was only ever borrowed in the first place.

lines: Here's what actually happens when that moment arrives.
Every last piece of that cached data gets cleared out, completely, to make room.
And even with all of that space freed up, the work that needed it still ends up writing some of what it's doing out to disk anyway.
Now try the exact same thing again, except this time keep that cached data under its own guaranteed floor the whole time, instead of letting it grow past it.
Run the identical pressure against it.
Nothing moves. Not one piece of it gets touched, start to finish.

Now a completely different pair of failures. One is a plain error thrown from inside a running process. The other is a decision made from outside that process, that it's gone over some limit and has to be stopped.
From the point of view of the thing actually doing the work, do those two look the same?
steps.answer: Not even close. One of them leaves behind a real, readable account of exactly what happened. The other leaves nothing behind at all.

lines: Here's the proof, side by side.
The plain error shows up as a genuine, catchable failure, with a complete trail showing precisely where it happened.
The outside decision leaves no trail anywhere. The process is simply gone, with nothing left behind to explain why.
Here's the reason those two things need two completely different fixes.
The error that happens from inside only ever has visibility into its own house: the space it was explicitly given to work with.

The decision made from outside is watching a much bigger picture, one that the thing doing the work was never able to see in the first place, which is exactly why growing its own space alone doesn't fix a failure it never saw coming.
Put both of these failures next to each other, coming from the same underlying cause: simply running out of room.
One of them hands you an exact account of what went wrong and where.
The other hands you silence, and a process that's no longer there to ask.
So there's one shared pot, split by a single movable line rather than a fixed wall, with a floor that genuinely protects whichever side needs it.

And there are two separate ways to simply run out of room entirely, each one leaving behind a completely different kind of evidence, which is exactly why each one calls for its own, different kind of fix.
